PREFACE.

It will be difficult for even the kindliest disposition to give a friendly welcome to the medical philosophy of Saxon days. As man has an ever-recurring tendency to make himself the standard of truth, to condemn, sneer at, and despise all that he does not choose or is unable to understand, so in an even greater degree every generation of men admires its own wisdom, skill, science, art, and progress. It claims as its own whatever it has learned from men of earlier times, and counts the few improvements that have originated in its own era as triumphs and distinctions that raise it above all that came before.

If we consider the history of ages past, these lofty pretensions will soon lose some of their confidence. The progress of those contrivances that contribute to our comfort, which we sum up in the word civilization, has been very slow and laborious. Our great capitals are smaller than Rome; the fortunes of our wealthiest men are trivial compared to the wealth of a Crassus or a Lucullus; our houses are less carefully heated in winter than the Roman villas; our poetry has no Homer, our sculpture no Praxiteles, our architecture no Parthenon; our philosophy has never seen a century like that between Pericles and Alexander. Those hundred years of Attic wit and wisdom have given us an education in dead languages and in the customs and manners of two thousand years ago, and are driving our native words from our tongues and making them unfamiliar to our ears.

This is page x of the Preface.

The Saxons accept Greek and Latin learning.

The same victory over future ages that puts into our children's hands a Virgil, a Demosthenes, a Horace, produced a similar effect upon our forefathers. When their driving, conquering, advancing spirit brought them into the island of the Britons and delivered the careless Celtic tribes to them as prey, they also found it worthwhile to inquire into this system of Latin knowledge, which raised fertile crops of wheat to feed every mouth, built houses that gave warmth against the storm, and brought from foreign distant lands remedies and aids for health and disease. Like us, they became students of Latin and Greek. They had of course already learned something of southern arts before, but when they arrived and became owners of territories that had been improved by the southerners, they could only fully enjoy their new acquisitions by understanding the methods by which they were managed.

Indigenous botany of the Teutonic races.

The Gothic nations had knowledge of their own regarding the kinds and properties of plants — that is, they possessed the more useful practical part of botany. This is clearly proved by the great number of native plant names found in the works now printed, in glossaries, and in the Gothic languages generally. Their medicine must have consisted partly in applying the properties of these plants to healing purposes, for otherwise the study would have had no real utility. The uses of hemp and liquorice were first learned by the Greeks from the Scythians. The Saxons evidently were also willing to rely heavily on amulets and incantations, for while these practices are accepted by the later Greek physicians, they appear much more frequently as the northern nations gained a wider foothold in the Roman empire.

¹ Herodotus, Book IV, Chapter 74. Theophrastus, Historia Plantarum, Book IX, Chapter 15.

PREFACE. xi

From the cradle modern Englishmen are taught to fight an angry battle against superstition, and they treat a talisman or a charm with some disdain and much contempt. But let us reflect that these playthings tended to quiet and reassure the patient, to calm his temper, and soothe his nerves — objects which, if we are not misinformed, the best practitioners of our own day willingly obtain by such means as are available to them. Whether a wise physician will deprive a humble patient of his roll of magic words, or take from his neck the fairy stone, I do not know; but this is certain: that the Christian Church of that early day, and the medical science of the empire, by no means refused the use of these arts of healing, these balms of superstitious origin. The reader may enjoy a laugh at such devices, but let him remember that dread of death and wakeful anxiety must be quieted by some means, for they are very unfriendly to recovery from disease.

Some part of the prevailing superstition must have partly originated from the Magi, for we find them ordering that the modern feverfew, the Pyrethrum parthenium, must be pulled from the ground with the left hand, that the fevered patient's name must be spoken aloud, and that the herbalist must not look behind him.

Pliny says also that the Magi and the Pythagoreans had many foolish tales about the eryngium, known in England as sea holly. That they ordered the pseudo anchusa to be gathered with the left hand, the name of the one who was to benefit from it to be uttered, and that it should be tied on a man for tertian fever. They used the aglaophotis, or peony, for the evocation of spirits. They got cures for

xii PREFACE.

headache, bleared eyes, dim sight, cataracts, growths in the eyes, toothache, rheumatism, quartan fevers, gout, spasms, lumbago, sterility, ghosts and nightmares, frenzy, family discord, indifference to wives, epilepsy, snakes, shiverings, darts, barking of dogs, fascination, gripes, kidney stones, childbirth, magic arts, mad dogs, dysentery, poison, tyranny, effeminacy, and a potent love charm — a "Come follow me, girls" — made from the hyena: but the hyena must be caught when the moon is in Gemini.¹

The Magi had a special admiration for the mole; if anyone swallowed its heart while it was still beating and fresh, he would immediately become an expert in divination.² The heart of a hen, placed upon a woman's left breast while she sleeps, will make her reveal all her secrets.³ The Roman calls this a monstrous lie — perhaps because he had tried it. The Magi were also the originators of the practice of searching for red or white stones in the nests of young swallows, a practice mentioned by our Saxon writers.⁴ A madman (lymphatus) would recover his senses if sprinkled with the blood of a mole; and those troubled by nocturnal spirits and by Fauns would be relieved if smeared with a dragon's tongue, eyes, gall, and intestines boiled down in wine and oil.⁵ Bull's dung was good for men suffering from dropsy, cow's dung for women.⁶

The Magi also taught men to drink the ashes of a pig's penis in sweet wine, and thereby to urinate into a dog's kennel, adding the words "lest he, like a hound, should make water in his own bed."⁷ If a man urinated a little on his own foot in the morning, it would protect him against harmful medicines — doses intended to harm him. For quartan fevers, they catch with the left hand a beetle that has

² Ibid. xxx. 7 = 3.
³ Ibid. xxix. 26.
⁴ Ibid. xi. 79.
⁵ Ibid. xxx. 24 = 10.

PREFACE. xiii

reflected antennae, and make an amulet of him. For sleep, the gall of a sacrificed goat smeared on the eyes or placed under the pillow was considered effective.

Demokritos was a devoted follower of the teaching of the Magi, "the most devoted student of the magicians." He wrote of an herb whose root, made into pills and swallowed in wine, would make guilty men confess everything, tormented at night by strange visions of the spirit world. Another herb, the "food of Gods," kept the kings of Persia in health and mental vigor. The "gospel plant" was drunk by the Magi before divination. The "laughter plant" produced phantoms and laughter, which could only be stopped by eating pine nuts, pepper, and honey in date wine. They also had an herb for producing handsome and good children. A disciple of Demokritos, Apollodoros, possessed a plant that could revive old love, even love that had turned to hatred. All these had magical names. Pliny's view of the general standing of the Magi's doctrine was that it was, of all the sciences found across the globe, the most fraudulent — which, it should be noted, is saying quite a lot — and that it owed its acceptance to its incorporating within itself the three most influential sciences among men: medicine; and religion, in whose darkness, Pliny says, the human race is still entangled (to call it superstition would be too modern a term); and mathematics, that is to say, astronomy.

Pythagoras held that the entire air is full of spiritual beings, who send men dreams and the signs of disease and health; and not to men alone, but to sheep and other livestock as well; and that for these spirits, purification rituals, averting ceremonies, and invocations are naturally devised.

xiv PREFACE.

and the like. He taught that holding anethum, that is dill, in the hand, is good against epilepsy. Pythagoras was the founder of the healing art among the Hellenic peoples.

Pythagoras taught that water would freeze with the herbs coracesia and calycia, also the flower of the aquifolia or holly. Chrysippus held that an animal nobody knew anything about, the phryganium, was a good amulet for quartan fevers. Cato held that a man would go comfortably to sleep after eating hare; and Plinius says there must be something in the general persuasion that after eating hare a man is good looking for nine days.

Serapion of Alexandria flourished (278 BC) forty years after the death of Alexander the Great, and was one of the chiefs of the Empiric school, who relied upon observation and experiment in preference to speculation and careful reasoning; yet he in epilepsy prescribed the warty excrescences on the forelegs of animals, camels' brain and gall, rennet of seal, dung of crocodile, heart of hare, blood of turtle, stones of boar, ram, or cock.

Soranos, an early writer of the methodic school, while he refused incantations as cures for diseases, testifies in so doing to their prevalence: — "Others approved the use of chants, as even the brother of Philistion records in book xxii on remedies, writing that a certain flute-player sang over painful places, which, when they leaped with the rhythm, were relieved as the pain was dispersed. Others again attributed this kind of remedy to Pythagoras."

[Footnote 1: That all the air is full of souls, and that from these are sent to men both dreams and signs of disease and health; and not only to men but also to sheep and other cattle. And that to these are directed both purifications and averting-spells, and all divination and omens and the like. — Diogenes Laertius, Life of Pythagoras, 32.]

PREFACE. XV

"They report having discovered this: but by the judgment of Soranus, those who believed that the strength of passion could be excluded by rhythms and song seem to be boasting out of mental vanity."

Pliny records that the rule is to sow basil with curses and ugly words; that pills of elaterium, the powerful juice of a wild cucumber, hung about the waist in rams wool, help childbirth, if the patient knows nothing about the remedy; he knew a man of praetorian rank, a chief man in Spain, who was cured of intolerable disorders of the uvula by carrying hung around his neck on a thread a root of purslane; that Sappho fell in love with Phaon because he found a masculine root of eryngium; that an amulet made of the seed of tribulus cures varicose veins; that tradition holds that men afflicted with tertian fever are relieved of it if they tie onto themselves a root of autumnal nettle, provided that when the root is dug the sick man's and his parents' names are duly spoken aloud; that if a man carries a poplar wand in his hand he will not get his legs chafed; the herb selago, which resembled savine, was gathered without use of iron, with the right hand, in pickpocket fashion, poked through the left armhole of the tunic, wearing a white robe, with bare clean washed feet, after an offering of wine and bread. Since ordinary "clinical" medicine is of no use in quartan fevers, he will tell us how to cure it by amulets; by the dust in which a hawk has been rolling himself, tied up in a piece of cloth with a red thread; by the longest tooth of a black dog; by a solitary wasp caught in the left hand.

xvi PREFACE.

and tied on; by the head of a viper cut off, or its living heart cut out, wrapped in a piece of cloth; by the snout and tips of the ears of a mouse placed in a rose-coloured patch, with the animal itself then let loose; by the right eye of a living lizard gouged out and placed in a bit of goatskin; by the ball-rolling dung beetle (scarabaeus stercorarius); a holly planted in the courtyard of a house keeps off witchcraft; they say that an amulet made from the spurge laurel (Daphne laureola, D. mezereum) will cure the white film "albugo" in the eyes, provided the plant is gathered before sunrise and the purpose is spoken aloud; an herb picked from the head of a statue and tied up in a red thread will cure headache; an herb over which dogs urinate, if pulled up without touching it with iron, cures dislocations. Enough, perhaps, has been said to characterize the collections of Pliny.

Josephus. Pliny was contemporary with Joseph, or Josephus. The tales about the mandrake that appear much later, and are found in the Saxon Herbarium, can be traced back to what he says of the Baaras, a plant that runs away from anyone who wants to gather it and will not stop until one throws upon it a woman's urine or menstrual blood — for foulness is often an element of mysteries — and even then it kills the dog that pulls it out. It is not certain that the mandrake berries are what is meant in Genesis 30:14.

Philagrios. Philagrios (364 A.D.) thought it superfluous and unseemly to add to a prescription a direction to spit once into the drug pot and once on the ground, along with some barbarous names, since without the names the remedy would be equally effective.

PREFACE. xvii

Xenokrates, who according to Galenos flourished two generations, or sixty years, before him, writes with an air of confidence about the good effects to be obtained by eating the human brain, flesh, or liver; by swallowing in drink the burnt or unburnt bones of the head, shin, or fingers of a man, or his blood. He also had a good list of nasty prescriptions, for which the veil of a dead language is required.

Galenos is cited by Alexander of Tralles as paying reluctant homage to incantations. His words perhaps do not go further than the conclusions of an unprejudiced physician of our own day might reach, were he willing to brave the quickly rising charge of superstition. "Some think that incantations are like old wives' tales, as I too did for a long while. But at last I was convinced that there is virtue in them by plain proofs before my eyes. For I had trial of their beneficial operation in the case of those stung by scorpions, and no less in the case of bones stuck fast in the throat, immediately thrown up by an incantation. And many of them are excellent, severally, and they reach their mark."

Pamphilos makes Galenos angry with his gypsy trickeries: "his old wives' tales, his Egyptian quackeries, his babbling incantations used by the folk employed to collect plants, his charms, and his humbugs — not merely useless, not merely unprofessional, but all false; no good even to little boys, not to say

xviii PREFACE.

"students of medicine." Pamphilos had written in alphabetical order about herbs.¹

Alexander of Tralles. Alexander of Tralles (A.D. 550) frequently prescribes periapts, that is, amulets, and wise words: thus for colic, he guarantees by his own experience and the approval of almost all the best doctors, dung of a wolf, with bits of bone in it, if possible, shut up in a pipe, and worn during the paroxysm, on the right arm, or thigh, or hip, taking care it touches neither the earth nor a bath. A lark eaten is good. The Thracians pick out its heart, while alive, and make a periapt, wearing it on the left thigh. A part of the caecum of a pig prepared with myrrh, and put up in a wolf's or dog's skin, is a good thing to wear. A ring with Hercules strangling a lion on the Median stone, is good to wear.² A bit of a child's navel, shut up in something of silver or gold with salt, is a periapt which will make the patient entirely at ease. Have the setting of an iron ring made octagonal, and engrave upon it, "Flee, Flee, Ho, Ho, Bile, the Lark was searching;" on the head of the ring have an N³ engraved: this is potent, and he thinks it would be strange not to communicate so powerful an antidote, but begs it may be kept from casual folk, and told

¹ Thus Pamphilos composed his treatise on plants. But that man turned aside to the myths of old women and certain Egyptian nonsense, together with the incantations which people recite as they gather plants. And indeed he made use of these for amulets and other tricks that were not merely meddlesome and outside the medical art, but entirely false. We, however, will speak of none of these things nor of their further foolish transformations. For we do not consider such myths to be at all useful even to small children, much less to those who are eager to pursue the work of medicine. And it seems to me that Hippocrates spoke at the very beginning of his Aphorisms the words "Life is short, the art is long," for the purpose of not wasting time on useless things.

Galen, de facult. simpl., lib. vi. p. 792, ed. Kühn.

² A Gnostic device. See Montfaucon, plates 159, 161, 163.

³ The N on the ring is Gnostic; see Montfaucon, t. cl., clxix., clxxvii.

Only to such as can keep secrets, and are trusty (lovers of virtue). For gout he recommends a certain cloth — a maiden's first menstrual rag, unwashed — also the sinews of a vulture's leg and toes tied on, making sure the right side goes to the right and the left to the left; also the ankle bones of a hare, leaving the poor creature alive; also the skin of a seal for use as soles; also a line of Homer, "the assembly was in uproar, and the earth groaned beneath," written on gold leaf when the moon is in Libra; also a natural magnet found when the moon is in Leo. Write on gold leaf, during the waning of the moon: "mei, threu, mor, for, teux, za, zon, the, lou, chri, ge, ze, ou, just as the sun is consolidated in these names and is renewed every day, so consolidate this plaster as it was before, now, now, quick, quick, for, behold, I pronounce the great name in which consolidated things rest in repose, iaz, azuf, zuon, threux, bain, chook, consolidate this plaster as it was at first, now, now, quick, quick." Then bits were to be chopped off a chameleon while it still lived, and the creature was to be wrapped in a clean linen rag and buried facing the sunrise, while the chopped-off bits were to be worn in tubes; all of this to be done during the waning of the moon. Then again for gout, some henbane, when the moon is in Aquarius or Pisces, must be dug up before sunset using the thumb and third finger of the left hand, and these words must be spoken: I declare, I declare, holy wort, to thee; I invite thee tomorrow to the house of Fileas, to stop the rheum of the feet of M. or N.; and say: I invoke thee by the great name, Jehovah, Sabaoth, the God who steadied the earth and stayed the sea, the filler of flowing rivers, who dried up Lot's wife and made her a pillar of salt — take the breath of thy mother earth and her power, and dry the rheum of the feet or hands of N. or M. The next day, before sunrise, take a bone of some dead animal and dig the

XX PREFACE.

root up with this bone, and say, I invoke thee by the holy names Iao, Sabaoth, Adonai, Eloi, and put on the root one handful of salt, saying, "As this salt will not increase, so may not the disorder of N. or M." And hang the end of the root as an amulet on the sufferer, etc. For agues, "the little animal that sits and weaves with the view to catch flies, tied up in a rag, round the left arm, is good." Trallianus mostly wrote very good sense. The Gnostics professed a medley of all the religions they could hear of.

Alexander Trallianus also recommends for epilepsy, from Asklepiades the pharmacist, a metal cross, a cruciform nail, tied as an amulet to the arm. He obtains from Zalachthes and Osthanes, interpreters of the Magi, a recommendation to try jasper and coral, with root of nux vomica in a linen cloth. Demokrates, an Athenian, who consulted the Delphic oracle, was told to get some worms out of a goat's brain. The occipital bone of an ass's head in a skin is also a good amulet. Get a big rivet from a wrecked ship, make a brooch of it, and insert a bone cut from the heart of a living stag.

The arts of magic — real arts, with effects visible to the eye, sciences, if the modern breadth of language be allowable — had at a very early period arrived at high perfection in Egypt, when Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses and Aaron, turning their rods into serpents, and water into blood (1600 B.C.); in Syria, when the witch or ventriloquist of Endor promised her clients conferences with the dead (1100 B.C.); in Hellas, when Ulysses visited the spirit world, and Circe turned men into swine (1100 B.C.); and in Persia, beyond chronological limits.

¹ Id. pp. 198, 199. That curious Gnostic charm seemed to deserve quotation at length.
² Id. p. 234, a small living creature.
³ Alex. Trall., lib. i. pp. 82, 83, 84, ed. 1556.

PREFACE. xxi

The practical wisdom of such men as Hippokrates, and the Epicurean skepticism of the age of Horace, had reduced the influence of magicians among educated minds to some reasonable limits. The revival of their power has been attributed to the depressing effect of imperial tyranny; but a larger share is probably due to the inroad of barbaric minds which the calm light of knowledge had not reached.

Saxons, Angles, and all the Gothic races were wholly unable to accept, to use, to learn the medical skill of Greece and of its pupil Italy. The point to which surgery had been brought was high; and if we don't say the same of medicine, perhaps we are not very good judges, having discovered very few remedies of our own. Our measure of their proficiency will be much safer in surgery than in pharmacy.

It seems pretty well agreed by competent and careful critics that the book on Wounds of the Head is by the great Hippokrates, who flourished at Kos during the Peloponnesian war (active 436, died 377?). He used a small drill, called a small trepan, which implies also some greater saw, which had a circular motion, and which is judged by medical men to be the trephine, and a jagged saw, which is held to be the trepan, and he gives careful directions to the operator to withdraw the instrument frequently and cool both it and the bone with cold water, and to take all care not to wound the lining membrane. The employment of splints on broken limbs is not of much note here, as we find our Saxons could adopt that resource. In the opinion of Dr. Greenhill, the Oath in the works of Hippokrates may be his; according to the last editor of his works, it is his, or of the Koan school.

¹ Hippokr. p. 907, 913, fol. ed. 1615. Sprengel, Attempt at a Practical History of Medicine, vol. i. p. 425.
² Hippokr. as above, p. 755.

xxii PREFACE.

school; it is a remarkable document, as laying down the outlines of professional etiquette, of the broad line of distinction between the physician and surgeon, and for its plain statement that cutting for the stone was then practised. The process is spoken of as familiar, and its dangers are shortly expressed by Aretaeus (A.D. 81), who observes that men sometimes die the very day of the operation, which, however, is indispensable. The same author mentions the relief afforded to those afflicted with the stone by the use of the catheter. Philagrios described in his lost works his own treatment of a case, where the calculus had escaped from the bladder and stuck fast in the ureter, so that the man, with suppression of urine and with pain, had almost died. The stone had made its way almost to the opening of the canal, but with a fine pair of forceps could not be extracted, nor yet by gently moving it with a probe. He would not cut the urethra from below, because that would certainly result in an artificial and inconvenient urinary opening, but he cut down upon it from above. Celsus, in the case of a large stone, recommends, as a matter of course, that it should be crushed by the instrument invented by Ammonios, the stone-cutter, or surgeon, who gave his chief attention to this subject, and of course before his own time (A.D. 15.) Ammonios is supposed to have practised at Alexandria.

Footnotes: I will not cut those suffering from the stone, but will give way to practitioners skilled in this work. Aret. Chronic. book ii. chapter 4. Id. Acut. book ii. chapter 9. Philagrios in Aetios. col. 551, in Med. Art. Principes. The original is unpublished. It is done in this way: a hook is inserted into the calculus, so as to hold it firmly and prevent it from rolling back; then an instrument of moderate thickness is applied, fine at the first part but blunt, which when brought up to the calculus and struck from the other side, breaks it; great care being taken that the instrument does not reach the bladder itself, nor that any fragment of the calculus causes injury. Celsus, book vii. chapter 26. 3.

PREFACE. xxiii

Asklepiades (B.C. 100), in extreme cases of difficult respiration from whatever obstruction of the trachea, cut through the air tube of the throat. Antyllus wrote down the proper directions for even a timid operator.

We find described in the Museo Borbonico some surgical instruments of bronze discovered in Herculaneum and Pompeii. There is the speculum magnum matricis, or "dioptrion," with two branches and a travelling yoke for them driven by a screw, for visual examination of the organic state of the uterus; it served rather as a dilator than as a speculum, and has been superseded by a better instrument, the invention of Recamier. Its careful use is described by Paulus Ægineta. There is also the speculum ani, or "dioptra," composed of two branches bent at right angles and opening by pressure on the handles: this instrument was known as "katoptir" to the author of the book on hemorrhoids among the works of Hippokrates. Further, a forceps of curious construction has been found, suited for removing pieces of bone from the surface of the brain in cases of fractured skull. It has been specially considered by Prof. Benedetto Vulpes [1847], who thinks it may also have been intended to grasp an artery. The Greeks, he observes, as appears by an inscription dug up near Athens, were able to tie an artery in order to stop hemorrhage, and words implying as much are found in a treatise of Archigenes (A.D. 100), existing in manuscript in the Laurentian library at Florence: "apobrocthion oun e"

xxiv PREFACE.

The vessels carrying blood towards the incision must be tied or sewn up. Near the end of the sixteenth century a French surgeon was the first to recover the technique of tying the artery, and the instrument he used was very similar (very closely resembling) the forceps in the Museum at Naples.

Forceps.     A curious pair of forceps has also been found, without parallel among modern surgical instruments; the blades have a half turn, and the grip is toothed and spoon-shaped when closed. By its construction it is suited for introduction into some internal cavity, and for holding firm and fast some growth there. Professor Vulpes finds it well suited for dealing with the growths which develop upon the Schneiderian membrane covering the nasal bones, or such as appear on the periphery of the anus or the orifice of the female urethra; especially those having a large base that cannot be tied off.

A tap.     There is further an instrument for draining dropsical fluid, described by Celsus and Paulus Ægineta. It was somewhat altered in the middle of the seventeenth century by Petit.

Another tap.     An instrument suited to draw off dropsical fluids a little at a time on successive days, as Celsus and Paulus Ægineta recommend, has also been dug up. Rust and compacted earth, which cannot safely be removed, have blocked the canal of the artifact and make conclusions less certain.

The Probe,     The probe, called "specillum" in Latin and μήλη in Greek, is reported by Cicero to have been invented by the Arkadian Apollo, who

also was the first to bind up a wound. Seven varieties are illustrated in the work of Professor Vulpes on one plate, with ends that are obtuse, spoon-shaped, flat and oval, flat and square, and flat and divided. The obtuse knob was called pyrene; the spoon type was called kyathiskos; those with a flat extremity were called spathomелai; and those with a knob at each end were called dipyrena.

The catheter of the ancients is illustrated by the same writer. It was fitted with a piece of wood to be drawn out by a thread, in order to prevent the obstructive effects of capillary attraction and to retrieve the urine after the instrument was withdrawn. It is made of bronze, and elastic catheters appear to be a modern invention.

They have, or had in 1847, eighty-nine specimens of pincers in the Naples Museum; fifteen are like what are now called anatomical pincers, only one has the form of the tenaculum, and seventeen are depilatory pincers. One pair of nippers is rectilinear, ending in points like a pair of compasses. Their names were labides and volsellae.

Hooks, called hamuli or ankistra, fourteen in number, had been stored in the cases in 1847; also a trident for cauterizing, and a spatula. A silver lancet was found during excavation accompanied by a small spoon, suited, as medical professionals agree, for examining a small quantity of flowing blood. There are also cupping vessels of a roughly spherical shape, from which air was expelled by burning a small amount of tow. A fleam for bleeding horses, of the same shape as that currently used, and a bent lever of steel, called a mochлikon or vectiarius, for lifting the bones of the skull in cases of depression caused by fracture. Professor Vulpes has provided us with illustrations of eight steel or iron knives for various surgical purposes, and of

a small plate suitable in the form of its handle for the application of cautery by fire.

A drug. There exists a tract of twelve pages by Dr. Simpson of Edinburgh, "On some ancient Greek medical vases for containing Lykion" [1856]. He knows "of four ancient vases or drug bottles intended to contain this valued eye medicine," "the Lykion Indikon of Dioscorides." They are severally labeled Lykion from Mousaios, Lykion from Herakleios [for Lykion], Lykion from Iason (two). The drug is the rusot or ruswut of India, an inspissated extract prepared from the wood or roots of several species of berberis, such as berberis lycium, aristata, etc. It is "most useful in all cases of inflammation of the external tunics of the eye." The vases in which it was found are of very small dimensions, and in three of them the internal content is much smaller than the external promise; this arose, of course, from the high price of the drug.

Northern medicine. Beside these elaborate contrivances and this skilful audacity of the Mediterranean peoples, northern medicine shows to no advantage. Bede, one of our safest and earliest authorities, gives an account of a leech, Cynifrid, or Cyneferth, who, in AD 679, opened a tumor for Ætheldryth, queen and abbess, without saving her life.

The name and office of leeches was familiar to the people: the Leechbook, or Liber Medicinalis, is intended for the use of a physician, not of a layman; and the frequent expression, "as leeches know how," shows that they received a professional education.

Resources. These leeches then, unable to use the catheter, the probing knife, the stone-crushing hammer, and ignorant of the far-sought Indian drugs, were in their early practice almost wholly thrown back upon the lancet,

PREFACE. xxvii

wherewith to let blood, and the "parabilia," the easily obtained remedies — the accessibles, chiefly plants from the field and garden. Not only the Angles and Saxons, the warrior inhabitants of our own island, but also all the races of Gothic invaders, were too uncivilized to learn much of Galen, or of Alexander of Tralles, though they would gladly have done so. The writings of Marcellus, called Empiricus, the Herbarium of Apuleius, the material current under the name of Sextus Placitus, the copious volumes of Constantinus Africanus, the writings of St. Hildegard of Bingen, the collections drawn from Dioscorides, the smaller Saxon pieces — all are of one character, substituting for surgical instruments and Indian drugs, native herbs, the plants of the homeland, ointments, and magical chants. Across the whole face of Europe, while the old Greek medical tradition survived in Arabia, the nearest available resource became the established remedy, and the careful incision of the skilled anatomist was replaced by a droning song.

The triumphant barbarians had no Paean, no Aesculapius, no Chiron, and far less a Hippocrates. That they must have used herbs before their sweep down over the south seems beyond dispute, and physicians are not only Teutonic in the form of their name, but are recorded as practicing a profession even in the most primitive ages.

What is now called "morbific virus" was with them called "venom;" epidemics were produced by "flying venom;" there was also "red venom," which suggests scarlet fever, "watchet venom," "white venom," "livid venom," and so on — all no doubt appropriate names.

The state of feeling about sorcery among these northern peoples is best gathered from a reading of the elder Edda, which is a world of witchery; the Gods themselves were truly described as charm smiths. We may perhaps wonder at the hold the Church had over people during the earlier ages of our modern period — at the saying of medicine masses, at the blessing of herbs taken from the field, at the placing of them upon the altar — but the Church had delivered men from a worse servitude than this, from the tyranny and terror of the poisoner and the wizard. The conscious helplessness of man, when the hand of God is upon him, must gladly humble itself in the dust and lick the dirt while craving mercy. Let the scornful reader, in good health, not toss his head on high at the so-called superstition of the simple Saxon, but consider rather how audacious an infidel that man would have seemed, in those ages, who had refused to pray in the accepted manner for the restoration of his health.

Effects, bad. Charms that act on the mind of the person being charmed always have some effect; in the case of incantations, commonly a harmful one. Hearne, the traveller in North America, relates somewhere that, being asked by an Indian to give him a charm against an enemy, and being convinced of the harmless folly of such sorceries, he complied and drew on a sheet of paper some circles, signs, and words. The Indian who received this took care that the doomed man should know about it; the man immediately sickened and before long died. Hearne resolved to make no more magic papers.

Hopeful of its power, she refrained from shedding tears, and her eyes recovered. But some zealous enemy of sorceries attacked her for the wickedness of getting well in this way; and prevailed

The Catholic Church of the day, unequal to rooting out these superstitious and rarely beneficial ideas, tried to throw a cloak of religion around them, invoking holy names to drive out devils by exorcism.

The Saxon physician, therefore, had he been as cool-headed as Hippocrates, as epicurean as our friend Horace, must have bowed before the fashion of the day and lamented his patients' notions. Possibly the makers of magic gibberish were as skeptical as men now are of its efficacy: but what did that matter? The leechbook had to adapt itself to its time.

In considering the special forms of popular belief, it is fitting that the Nightmare, in which men still believe, should come first. "Mare" in that combination is something like Genius or Spirit; it occurs in Woodmare, which was the Saxon name for Echo. From the accounts we have of the importance attached to its effects, it may be suspected that something beyond the symptoms of an uneasy sleeping position, or an undigested supper, must have been included in the term. Yet, while we habitually dismiss this terror by attributing the episode to careless eating, it is in itself, while it lasts, an ugly mental struggle, much more like an emissary from the sulfurous pit than an angel visiting from heaven. In the Hellenic world the Nightmare, as among our own forefathers, was considered as a god or a demigod, a god or a half-god, for the physician Soranus denies this popular belief, denies that it deserves a place among the diseases, passiones, or as men phrase it now, that it is worthy the attention of a pathologist, but declares it a mere disturbance of sleep. This calling a nocturnal horror by dismissive names does not dispose of its alarms. Themison of Laodikeia, (63 B.C.) called it the Throttler, Choker, "since it chokes the sick." Others commonly called it the Ephialtes, which means, I suppose, as Actuarius and the dictionaries say, the Jumper-on; and doctors tell us that the disorder deserves attention at the very outset, for its continuation is followed by insanity or epilepsy. Oribasios calls it a serious disease, and anticipates the same ill effects where it comes on every night, dwelling on those cases where it has its origin in the brain. Some of the most horrible of these visitations arise from the sympathies of night with mental agony in the day, but our authorities take no notice of these. To this night demon many passages in the works now published refer; not under the exact term Nightmare, but as "monstrous night visitors," and perhaps under the general term, "temptations of the fiend." The wider observation of medical authors taught them that this inconvenience grew in some patients into a disease, and the manner of treating all subjects belonging to the unknown — which prevailed among people whose imaginations were as lively as our own, and whose book learning was less — represented, whether truly or not (I say nothing), the same thing as the devil. One of the afflictions with which witchcraft tormented men was the Knot, by which a man was restrained so that he could not exercise his will with a woman. It was called in the Latin of the time Nodus and Obligamentum, and appears in the glossaries, translated by the Saxons into lyb, drug, φδρμακον, since the evil effect might be produced by such means. Gunnhilld put her hands round his neck and kissed him and said: "If I have as much power over thee as I intend, then I lay this upon thee, that thou may never come to fulfillment with the woman whom thou intendest there in Iceland; but thou shalt well frame thy will with other women. Traces of this philosophy — for it is more physiology than superstition — are to be found elsewhere. Pliny says that southernwood is most efficacious against all "acts of sorcery by which sexual intercourse is inhibited." Also that the seed of the tamarisk mixed in a drink or food with the urine of a castrated ox will put an end to sexual desire. Galen says that "priests eat rue and chaste-tree," apparently as a cooling remedy; for he says "and so the seed of rocket with honey and fenugreek given to a fasting man incapacitates him (he cannot have an erection)." "There are indeed many kinds of harmful magic, brought about by incantations, knots, and mental images. For some disturb the minds of men and compel them to succumb to violent emotional impulses, such as intense inborn love, or savage hatred, or terror and other mental torments. Others impede sexual acts; and so forth." We find protective charms "against harmful binding, as they are called." Priests are warned not to make alterations in the mode of conducting the marriage service by

Recipes for Knots. The processes in use for these mischievous purposes were of course secret, both as valuable possessions and as dangerous evidence against the doctor; and either as actual poisons or as ridiculous trash. But a few specimens are on record. "If you wish someone not to have intercourse and desire to make him slower in sexual performance, put fungi still living from a lamp that has gone out of its own accord into his drink, and hand it to him unknowingly to drink, and he will immediately be enfeebled." Again, "If you wish someone to be unable to have intercourse with a woman by night, place a crowned pestle under his bed."

Love charms. The wizard, witch, sorcerer, druggist, doctor, or medicine man was equally ready at securing affection. He played the part of a sort of ochreous Cupid. A man's death was sometimes brought about by the arts of the sorcerer, who was undoubtedly a true poisoner, compounding poisons when occasion required, but who was also supposed to work by incantation and fascination.

We are acquainted with the Nightmare, which, as appears from the German Mahr, may be a masculine word as well as feminine, and with the Woodmare, corresponding to the Greek Echo, who was a nymph. To translate various Greek words, the Saxon vocabularies mention mount elves, wood elves, sea elves, downs elves, land elves, and water elves. The Leechbook has a recipe for the "water elf disease, when the nails of the hands are livid, and the eyes watery and

"downcast;" the disease is to be cured by herbs and an incantation. It has another remedy for elf disease, with several prescriptions, for elf hiccup, the convulsive condition called lugmos by Greek medical authors. To the Latin of the Medicina de Quadrupedibus, on the subject of Dwarves, the translator has added a receipt against a Dwarf. These beings, when offended, were terrible. They seem to derive their name from the words meaning perverse, and in one glossary the word teter is translated as buenc. According to Grimm, the invisibility of the dwarves usually lies in some definite part of their clothing, in a hat or mantle, by the accidental removal or loss of which they suddenly become visible. The Dwarf tales mention nebelkappen, caps of darkness, grey frocks, and red caps, scarlet mantles. Earlier centuries employ the expressions hell cap, hell clothes, mist caps, and tarn caps. But, as appears, the dwarves of this book now printed are more like the fearful creations of the Edda.

Full faith of the Saxons. Beda had full faith in the claims of these witches to raise storms. He relates how Germanus and Lupus, bishops of Auxerre and Troyes, when sent by a church synod to Britain, were encountered by a "hostile force of demons," a hostile lot of demons, who raise storms and turn day into night, driving the bishops' vessel from its course, and flinging the waves over it. Lupus calls up Germanus, who felt somewhat unsettled by this tossing, and with the name of the Trinity and some drops of water the tempest is stilled.

Theodorus, archbishop of Canterbury, mentions this power of the witches: "If anyone is a sender of storms, that is, a sorcerer, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water."

It is related in the Herbarium, in an article on the Castor oil plant (article 176), where the name of the plant is probably taken from Dioscorides, and the prescription is due to the proverbial "stupidity of the Saxons," that this herb soothes every storm. The same is said of the aglaofotis (article 171).

Herbs generally provided the Saxons with their materials for healing all bodily ailments, though they sometimes drew on animals as well. Our own medicines are very largely taken from what we call the vegetable kingdom, but their composition is hidden from the patient by the mysteries of prescriptions and foreign names. A sick man thinks himself properly cared for if he happens to make out that his doses contain Taraxacum, Belladonna, Aconite, Hyoscyamus, or Arnica, or if he is refreshed with Ammonia; but he smiles contemptuously at the herb woman who administers dandelion, nightshade, wolfsbane, henbane, elecampane, or who burns horn in the sickroom. Perhaps herbs are more truly effective than we would easily believe. The locksmith at Teddington told me that he had broken the bone of his little finger, and for two months it was grinding and crunching, so that he felt sometimes quite unwell. One day he saw Dr. — go by, and told him about it; the doctor said, you see that comfrey there — take a piece of the root, chew it, put it on your finger, and wrap it up. The man did so, and in four days his finger was well. This story struck me all the more since comfrey is the "confirma" of the Middle Ages, and the "symphyton" of the Greeks, both names seeming to attribute to the plant the same binding and consolidating virtue. Beyond the examples in the medical treatises that survive — which are less distinctive since they are borrowed — we find the healing power of herbs spoken of as a matter of course. Thus: "There is no herb grown in wood or field that cannot ever sustain life

Some, for a baby's recovery, would creep through a hole in the ground and stop it up behind them with thorns; some, to secure health, would fast "in honour of the moon;" some would treat a sick child by witchcraft, or pull it through some earth at the crossways.

This text is already in English and requires no translation. It is a preface discussing errors made by Pliny and medieval translators when rendering Latin plant names into English. The author notes that Pliny made many mistakes, including incorrectly identifying cyprus as privet rather than Ligustrum. Translators of Latin botanical works faced great difficulty, as they did not always know which plant a Latin name referred to. For example, in the Herbarium, article xxix, the word Ostriago was rendered as "water elder," which is incorrect; the author believes it actually refers to the Ostrya tree known to Theophrastus and to modern botany. In article xxv, the word chamaelaia, meaning the Daphne mezereon, was confused with chamaeleon, a stalkless thistle, and translated as "wolf's comb," which is a thistle but a stalked one. Other mistranslations are noted: hedera nigra is far from earth ivy, Tribulus is not gorse, Strychnus is not foxglove, Sampsuchos is not elder, Capparis is not woodbind, and Iuniperus is not gorse. The most striking confusion, however, was the identification of Dymele, which by all its Teutonic connections should be the hop plant, with the poisonous Bryony. Any doubt about the correct lexicographical identification has been settled by the Saxon author himself, who, speaking on his own authority and not merely translating, says that this plant is so excellent that it is mixed into ordinary drinks, that is, into beer.

This page is already written in modern English and requires no translation. It is a preface (page lvi) discussing the reliability of an Anglo-Saxon herbal writer and translator, noting that the writer confused two plants — likely bryony and hop — an error shared as late as 1659 by Lovell in his Herball, and possibly originating with Pliny, who was unclear at the start of his 23rd book. Dioscorides, in speaking of white and black bryony as bearing grape-like clustered fruit, clearly could not have meant the hop, which bears no resemblance to grapes.

Once the translator's claim to infallibility is set aside, other identifications also come into question: "Atterlothe" (chapter xlv), despite being credited with remarkable properties, cannot be cock's-foot grass; and "Smearwort" (chapter xx), whose name in early Germanic languages suggests something greasy and buttery, cannot be Aristolochia, but must be Butterwort, Pinguicula.

It is, however, unreasonable to demand that a Saxon writer of nine hundred years ago give accurate renderings of foreign plant names — something that cannot even be achieved in the latter half of the nineteenth century, when leading authorities still disagree. Turning to the sources of the Leechbook, the question of how much the Saxons drew from Greek literature will arise urgently. The author of that work borrows a page at a time from Alexander of Tralles, Paullus of Aegina, and Philagrios. It will be more practical to address the specific details once the full Saxon text is available. In the meantime, some background materials for understanding the subject are worth providing. In a sense, children who learn the meanings of words like "system,"

"scheme," can be said to learn Greek, though the words do not appear in the proper alphabet. And in some sense our ordinary scholars may be said never to have seen a Greek book, since our Hellenic authors are scarcely ever printed in the true alphabet, but in an imitation of an Alexandrine or Byzantine cursive script, which neither Plato nor Aristophanes could have read to save his life. These considerations prevent us from rashly declaring that unless proof can be produced that the Saxons read Greek in the Greek script, they cannot properly be said to have read it at all. Let us agree to suppose that a Greek word written in the common English way, and correctly understood by its English equivalent, counts as a step toward knowledge of the Greek language, and we shall find that, as proved by the surviving glossaries, which cite Greek words by the hundreds, the Saxons had taken very many such steps and degrees of knowledge of that kind. Sometimes a Greek word is marked as such by the letter G. Not infrequently we find Hebrew words interpreted as well.

The Colloquium, now well known, was intended as an academic exercise — the Colloquium being educational in purpose — to instruct the student, and perhaps to test him, in some of the less straightforward words occurring in Latin conversation. That this was its purpose is confirmed by the words of Ælfric Bata, who added to a copy of the earlier Colloquium a piece of his own, "more difficult," as he himself says. Through the kindness of the Rev. Mr. Eld, librarian of St. John's College, Oxford, who allowed me the use of his rooms, I have been able to spend several days with the Oxford copy. The Colloquium itself, despite the claims of one of its editors, contains no Saxon glosses; it was therefore intended to be given to a class of students to be turned into English; and the Cot-

For the improvement of our acquaintance with what our forefathers were doing, I shall print the third piece, with its glosses, as far as I was able, in the bright days of summer, to read its blurred and worn record; and it will be seen that Greek words were taught to the students. Of the manuscript from which the text of the Herbarium and Medicina de Quadrupedibus has been taken — MS. V. — Bibl. Cotton, Vitellius C. iii., the reader has a specimen in the facsimile. Opinions gathered from those most experienced agree that it dates as a copy from about 1050 A.D. For myself, I only venture to believe that it was written out not earlier than A.D. 1000, nor later than the Conquest, 1066 A.D. It has been chosen as the groundwork of this edition, because it is illustrated by drawings in colours of the plants, an advantage which none of the other old English, or so-called Anglo-Saxon, copies possessed. While uninjured it must have been a regally magnificent book, executed at an enormous expense. It suffered from the fire at Ashburnham House, 1731, and, like the rest of the MSS., was taken out of the ashes a shrivelled blackened lump of leaves. Recently it has been rebound. The binder first soaked the ruins in water to make them limp; he then flattened them, and for this purpose was obliged often to cut through the edges, and to stretch them by pins,

The illustrated Latin manuscripts here mentioned were of interest chiefly as they shed light on the meaning of the Saxon drawings. Most botanists would turn away from them in scorn, declaring them unscientific; only those who take pleasure in investigating the history as well as the modern phase of their favourite science will give them any attention. B., a Bodleian manuscript, is a very handsomely written folio, twelve inches tall and eight broad, in double columns, with the letters clear and sharply marked, with vacant spaces intended for drawings of the plants and snakes, but never filled in. The interpretation of the English names of plants rests on the same general basis as the rendering of any other obsolete words. But lest my purpose be misunderstood, it is necessary to draw the readers' attention to the true state of the question. Until now, people have been content with what is found in dictionaries, and the dictionaries do nothing but quote as authorities such a book as this Herbarium, or some glossaries. The interpretation, therefore, is sometimes probably false due to errors in such books, and sometimes contradictory, because glossaries disagreed with one another. On discovering that the poisonous bryony, with its clusters of berries, is confused with the "humble," with its hop catkins and wholesome juices, it became impossible any longer to blindly follow the author before us. To determine, therefore, the meaning of any obscure English word, it was by no means appropriate to simply accept the Greek or Latin equivalent established in the Herbarium or elsewhere; one had to find out what plant was actually intended by such a word. Thus, if the Herbarium identifies Liðpyrt as Ostriago, and Ostriago proves probably to be 'Οστρύα, a tree not known in this country, while at the same time Liðpyrt is identified as Dwarf Elder by much concurrent testimony, the conclusion must be that our author was probably wrong in his identification. In glossaries, and to some extent here as well, the authors' aim was to convey as nearly as possible the sense of a foreign word to English-speaking readers; their translation was, therefore, often only an approximation. Liðpyrt for Ostringo, and for Erifia, may be excused on this ground. For Populus alba, Abele seems, at least,

not Latin, not "Albella," whether connected with the Polish bialy, meaning white, or not: the Populus tremula was the Æpr, the aspen, and in some glossaries is very reasonably called the Cpicbeam, quickbeam, as always alive: the Populus nigra is commonly now called the Italian poplar, and though admitted by our men of science as indigenous, is perhaps an importation. In the face of those native names it seems extraordinary to find the glossaries interpreting Populus as bync, birch, at the same time as Betulus, birch. Whatever the solution, I cannot accept from a glossator the teaching that Populus is birch. Perhaps by an emendation we may recover another native name. In Gl. R., p. 45, we have Saginus, hpıt hærel. Only one kind of Corylus is known in England; I propose Ægirus, Aiyeipos, for the white hazel. Sometimes the glossator did not at all know his plant under a foreign name, which must be excused by all who are not mere novices. Sometimes the inattention of editors misrepresents the old writer. In Gl. R., p. 47, is written,

Cedrus, cedar beam.
Cedria, cedar resin, [that is, the sap of it].

The editors never made this out; yet "Hissæpe Cedria" should not have found its way into any dictionary.

No interpretation of a significant name can be satisfactory unless the meaning well befits the plant. Smearwort, as mentioned above, must be a greasy plant, such as Butterwort is. Quickbeam has no sense whatever when applied to the Rowan tree, though the name is well rooted in our language; and it perhaps belonged originally to the Aspen, as some glossaries give it. Gl. Cresis, aspen tree, Tremulus,

which the editors have not printed. The Eglantine is the Sweetbriar with its aculei, sharp points, straight or

Sources.     The Herbarium consists of two parts: a translation from the work entitled Herbarium of Apuleius, with a few extra paragraphs; and a continuation, chiefly from Dioscorides. Ackerman and Sprengel, who have written on the history of medicine, and Sillig, who in his edition of Pliny has printed a short fragment of Apuleius, are of the opinion that Apuleius never wrote the book. Saumaise thought he did. Sprengel is angry at the book as unphilosophical, but it is better for being practical. Its translation into English shows its popularity, and amid the scarcity of old English manuscripts, four copies still exist of this work, and three glossaries show themselves indebted to it. Nothing is less permanent than science. The English translation is now published, doubtless as giving us better knowledge of what the Anglo-Saxons

The name Spreritis, Herbar. cxxxviii., is not in Dioskorides. But in a Latin manuscript of Trinity College, Cambridge, of late date, containing extracts from Dioskorides, it is found with the following description: "It has small woolly leaves from a single root; it sends out many branches along the ground, a saffron-colored flower resembling the ox-eye, and a myrtle-like scent when rubbed between the fingers." These are the very words of our Saxon text. Zamalentition is also to be found in the Trinity manuscript. It is therefore to be concluded that the translator did not draw directly from the Botanist of Anazarba. It is, however, to his credit that he drew from him at all. He was not entirely unphilosophical after all.

The Trinity manuscript, immediately after the last entry from Apuleius, indicates something of its own origin in these words: "Here begins the book of medicine of Dioskorides from the Hebrew sources." If the Saxon additions to Dioskorides and this manuscript came from a common source, we should be here taught that the Greek had filtered through a Hebrew text. But it is quite impossible that the names of the plants could retain their original form after being expressed in Hebrew characters.

On type forms and their value: The text has been printed in a form that preserves the shape of the characters as they appear in the original manuscripts. Beyond the objection to printing in the letterforms of our own day — an objection that arises naturally in anyone who dislikes dressing up antiquity in modern clothing — there is another objection that is not sentimental at all: by making everything uniform we lose all the chronological characteristics of a manuscript that arise from the shape of its letters. The age of an English manuscript can generally be determined to within half a century by the shape of certain letters. Print all these forms alike, and you, as far as it lies within your power, shut out from your readers the information contained in those forms. The letter ꝼ is a hallmark of an early English manuscript, one belonging probably to the ninth or tenth century. It may be seen in the facsimiles of the Lauderdale Orosius, of the Codex Exoniensis, and of the C.C.C. copy of the Chronicle. It occurs frequently in the Leechbook, but not in the copy of a lost chapter which we shall restore to its proper place — not because of the text itself, but because of the

copy made of it, is later than that of the rest of the book.

It appears from the inscription on Alfred's jewel that it was known under a certain form, in which I recognize a Hypsilon (Υ); it is, however, found in a manuscript of Alfred's time, as yet unpublished, in the common form. It does not occur at all in the manuscript of Cædmon, which is written throughout with y undotted. In saying this I do not include in the Cædmon — if it is Cædmon (for Pseudo-Cædmon is a strong assertion) — that piece on the Harrowing of Hell, which is bound up in the same volume, but written in a much closer hand, with about forty-eight, instead of thirty-nine letters in a line; this has y dotted. The letter in question does not occur in the Herbarium in any of the manuscripts.

Experts in manuscripts have finer and more delicate traits by which they distinguish the age of copies; these are so minute that a traced facsimile will scarcely reproduce them. Except these, and the ornamental letters, and the contractions, which are forbidden in this set of publications, the present text puts before the reader the manuscript as written. When the shape of letters affords so discriminating and so constantly present a test of the age of manuscripts, it is a subject of great regret to me that editors have so freely applied the sponge of modernism, wiping away all such peculiarities. In some cases we can immediately identify an interpolation from the original by watching this feature. Towards a reliable interpretation, the first step is an adequate grammar. A few remarks shall therefore be offered on this subject.

Vocalisation. The vocalisation of the oldest English manuscripts differs from what may be called the received standard, from the printed homilies of Aelfric, for instance, and from the grammars which are all based on Aelfric's Latin grammar. It is wholly a mistake to hold up the received method as the standard for the pure West Saxon dialect, as may be seen by appealing to the authorities. We have a manuscript which bears on the face of it satisfactory evidence of having been sent out of Alfred's court by his own directions. Accents. It is only partly true that the accentual mark in manuscripts denotes a long vowel. Of this I shall mention what I believe to be a decisive proof; but must first say that Mr. Thorpe wholly deceived himself when he supposed the accentuation of his edition of Cædmon, if it is Cædmon, to be like his original. He says, "In the accentuation, which confirms in almost every case the theory of Professor Rask, I have followed the authority of manuscripts, and except in a very few instances that of the manuscript of Cædmon itself." I add my testimony to that of others, that the accentuation has been much altered. In the original manuscript at page 14, line 11, equivalent to page 17, line 8 of Thorpe's edition, the word "þ́" is accented; the words are written thus: "þ́ him com." It is

It is evident that it was the emphatic sense and not any long vowel which brought the accent down on that word. The syllable un–, with the privative sense, is frequently accented, as marking a change of meaning. The word "Þondum" (except in Cædmon, if it is indeed Cædmon's manuscript) often receives the accent, but the vowel is certainly not an omega. In the old manuscripts the affix "dom" is accented, indicating here a long vowel, as in the German equivalent "-thum," but our language has a tendency to throw back accents, and "wisdom" must have long before become Wisdom. Some have thought that two concurrent syllables in English cannot take accents at once; but our utterance of "Rich man, Poor man," as compared with "Chapman" and "Helmsman," is irreconcilable with that theory. The page of Cædmon cited above gives us "hit him, ongan him, ahop, hir lic," with concurrent accents, in the original manuscript. These, observe, were not all vowels long in themselves. The Leechbook accents the inflexive syllable -um, as in "hatum, oppum, godum, pynctum," pronouncing, it may be presumed, this vowel long. This pronunciation must have disappeared before the manuscripts could confuse such forms as "þam ilcan" with "þam ilcum, minum, minon," which they very frequently do.

The Saxons accented Latin words as a guide to the reader; thus in MS. H., folio 94, we find "incantationibus, spandines, tempestates, omnipotentir narrcı": these are not all long vowels, though they are all long syllables. On folio 96 b, "hilajur" is an erroneous pronunciation.

Indifference of vowels. Final syllables with short vowels are written with e, i, o, or u. Hence a verb ending in -obon became, on dropping the N, -obe in its termination; and pærtmar, dropping the s, might become pærtme.

Final vowels dropped. The general analogies of the oldest English with Latin and Greek would lead us to expect the neuter plural to end in a short vowel such as a; so that ponba should represent verba; and this is so. But English also loses the vowel, and the plural becomes ponb. This is the case with most of our neuters. And not only that. Other terminations lose the vowels we expect to find. The adverbs ending in -on, and like -ther, meaning "from," are often found to have, and doubtless originally did, end in -one, as heonon, heonone, hence.

The omission of a final short vowel affects the orthography of nominatives: thus Kemble says, on ærende, "In later times the final e was sometimes omitted, but should not have been so." The word for pain (a masculine, not to be confused with the neuter word for work) is written in the nominative form twice in the manuscript of Cædmon. The forms meaning "goddess" lead us to suppose that the language had a feminine -ne ending for names of women's offices, as Dirne, Old German Diorna, famula, puella. The St. Johns Oxford manuscript gloss for monacha or monialis has mynecenu, which, and not mynecen, is the true form of the nominative. So that piln was perhaps once pilne, and þeznen, þinen, has lost a vowel. See fpnæc for fpnæce, Codex Exoniensis, p. 421, line 3.

The inflectional endings set out in grammars are, or ought to be, the forms normally observed in the language. In all less well-known languages, Greek included, the standard grammars are often substantially in error. In the oldest written English, misleadingly called Anglo-Saxon, these inflectional endings are less certain, since the writings have had few scholars; and we cannot be expected to take our rules from the grammars. Yet it would not be reasonable to favour a reading merely because it is exceptional: we dare go only so far as to accept more readily those less usual, less established forms which accord with the tendency of the period, which was to drop endings, as is seen in the English of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, the "Semi Saxon" and the "Early English" of conventional literary terminology. The infinitive meaning "to give thanks" is found in the Exeter book written without the N. These two passages carry more evidential weight than two agreeing manuscripts, and it follows that in the tenth century infinitives had already begun to drop the N. Feminine genitives in s. Some feminines made the genitives in s; perhaps irregularly, and from a desire in the writer to find some mode of marking the genitive distinctly; thus ea, meaning "a river," makes its genitive ear; "emnihter" means "of the equinox" in the treatise On Times; "dicer" occurs in the charters.

Of concurrent consonants. The early manuscripts, representing sounds more than modern fashionable spelling does, often omitted some one of many concurring consonants. Thus they wrote "pyntpuma," where derivation required "pynttpuma," so "ftpenðu" for "ftpenzðu," "pilbeop" for "pilb beop," "nemrt" for "nemnrt."

This suppression of consonants often, to a modern eye, confounded grammatical inflexions; "hie habbað me to heannan zecopene," Cædmon? MS. p. 15, line 15, meaning "they have chosen me to be chief"; instead of "zecopenne," which is the true syntax. "Beppeoh ðe peapme"; meaning "wrap thyself up warm," Leechbook, lib. I. cap. xlvii. 1, 2.

So as to be warm, the predicate is explainable by the Greek construction meaning "so as to be," which constantly occurs in Greek and other languages. "Wipe the table dry," where an adverb is quite out of place. He who must have on the journey a sound mind — Cod. Exon., p. 430, line 10, in the edition, for the form "runbne." The editor rightly supposes "hyge" to be masculine; it forms the genitive "hyges"; the Paris Psalter, lxviii. 6, has the masculine adjective "holbne" in Beowulf, 531; "minne" in Caedmon? MS. p. 19, line 21; and "hatne," Paris Psalter, lxxviii. 38. The passages in the same Paris Psalter, lxi. 8, 11, may be explained in more ways than one. This disguise of a masculine termination is very common in participles, since the syllables -enbne contain a combination which no one but an elocution master will produce from his lips with ease. Hence we explain "þnurenbe hyge," Cod. Exon., p. 165, 25, ed. Thus "ænne laman on bebbe licgenbe," Matth. ix. 2, where the Lindisfarne MS. has "liccenbe in bêþe," and the Hatton cuts off the final vowel: thus again, "he geseah ænne man sittenbe," Matth. ix. 9. "Beheold . . . . bynnende beam" — the people beheld a burning beam — Caedmon? MS. p. 148, line 4. I shall not multiply citations, for Kemble has already remarked, Beowulf, 92, Appendix, "umborwesende is the accusative singular. . . . Participles not infrequently have this anomaly and omit the n." Any combination of sound, however, which rendered the n of the accusative indistinct on the teeth gave occasion to a neglect of the unsounded letter by the scribe. "Deorol" is masculine in the Gospels; therefore "unclæne deorol," Luke iv. 33, stands for "unclænne." On "mine gehynad anrealbne geþoht," Beowulf, 508, Kemble says we must read "minne." Adjectives in the feminine.
The feminine nominative singular of adjectives ended, in remote times, in a short vowel, in full analogy with the Latin: this vowel is found occasionally with all forms, and is not confined to such words as are fair. "Here is a virgin, a ladylike maiden" (Cædmon? MS. p. 101, lines 19, 20); "to them a ladylike maiden in beauty to many proud ones she seemed" (id. p. 89, line 15); "longsome love" (id. p. 91, line 4). Numerous examples occur in Rawlinson's Boethius, and he had no theories nor pledged opinions to defend.

An adjective placed immediately in juxtaposition with a substantive or another adjective could dispense with its case inflection. The examples are very numerous, but most of them have been disposed of by the hyphen system, making them half compounds; in that treatment there is some truth, for a termination doing duty for two consecutive words, makes them draw very close to each other, and we have something of the same kind in such words as melancholia. But for myself, the representation of an adjective standing immediately before its substantive, as being more truly an approximation to a compound word than an epithet, is tolerable only in some examples, as in "small intestines," "small guts," "opened of kin," and these cases are distinguishable in spoken language by their having only one full accent on the group of syllables. Other instances, such as "a heap of eggs," raw eggs, "God sent a very great rain," God sent a heavy rain, do not commend themselves on this principle to my judgment. Even such phrases as "king almighty" are better sense, if treated as "eall" for "ealþa," than if considered as compounds.

I have before observed that the case ending –um becomes, by loss of the final consonant, –e. Rask had remarked this of adjectives, but the translator struck out his words. The change however is seen in substantives, and in short, it is a mere decay of termination.

Plural verbs in –e. In former treatises I have observed that by the loss of N, verbs plural in –on come to end in –e. By this simple explanation, harmonizing with other changes in our early language, we fully understand what has been called "a verb with a singular termination joined to a plural nominative," "a singular for plural."

Substantives out of adjectives. Adjectives become substantives, and are sometimes masculine, sometimes feminine, sometimes neuter.

Just as the Greek genitive "hudatos" means "some water" used partitively, so in Saxon English the genitive denotes "some of." An example of the partitive genitive occurs in Med. de Quad., viii. 6. In that passage, observe also that "swete" agrees either with "apulbne," which is feminine,¹ or with "wunde," whereas it is the apple that is sweet, and "appel" is masculine.

The Leechbook takes considerable licence with careless grammatical construction. In a list of the ingredients of a recipe it commonly uses nominatives, even though a verb requiring accusatives had preceded. It often constructs sentences as if we should say in Latin: "Given to the sick patient this medicine, fasting"; either because it is equivalent to "Let the sick patient drink this medicine while fasting," or from simple carelessness, or on the principle remarked above, that a grammatical ending was superfluous.

BETONY. I. Betonica officinalis. Botany.

1. This plant, which is called betony, grows in meadows, on open downlands, and in shady places. It is beneficial both for a man's soul and for his body: it protects him against monstrous nocturnal visitors and against frightful visions and dreams. The plant is very wholesome, and so you shall gather it in the month of August without the use of iron. The plant called wood berry, or madberry, grows on open downland and has leaves resembling a leek. One should gather a root of this plant around midsummer, and likewise the whole plant, as it is very useful for medicinal purposes.
